You report rumours and other people's claims with sollen (Er soll reich sein = he is said to be rich) and wollen (Er will ihn kennen = he claims to know him), in the present and in the past.
to terminate (a lease), to give notice
The house is said to have been sold.
He claims to have lived here.
He supposedly wants to throw out all the tenants.
Use “sollen” for rumours and information from others: Er soll reich sein = he is said to be rich.
Use “wollen” for claims about oneself that you doubt: Er will Arzt sein = he claims to be a doctor.
Form the past of these structures: soll / will + participle + haben / sein (Er soll hier gewohnt haben).
Tell the subjective meaning from the objective one (Er soll kommen = he is to come / Er soll gekommen sein = he is said to have come).
Use angeblich, es heißt, man sagt to distance yourself from a piece of information.
It's July 2031. Klaus is back from holiday and comes into the café “Bei Ingrid” with some news. Lena and Ludwig are listening.
Have you heard? The house at number thirty-three has been sold. To an investor from Munich.
Next to us? Who says so?
Mrs Becker from the kiosk. And he's said to be filthy rich. Apparently he's already bought ten houses in Berlin.
Mrs Becker. The same woman who claimed I was a spy in 1995.
Yes, all right. But this time it's true. Apparently the man wants to throw out all the tenants. He wants to renovate the flats and sell them at a high price.
That would be terrible. The Yilmaz family with three children live at thirty-three. And old Mrs Schulze, who has her coffee with me every morning.
And now comes the strangest part. The investor claims he grew up here. In Prenzlauer Berg. He even claims to know Ludwig.
Me? I don't know any investor from Munich. What's his name?
Michael Kühn. He's supposedly coming tomorrow to see the house.
Brandt… Brandt… There was a little Michael Kühn. In the nineties. He's said to have… no. It can't be the same one.
Nothing yet. But tomorrow I'll ask him. And then we'll know the truth, not just what Mrs Becker says.
1. “sollen” = is said to (rumour, information from others)
Besides “should / be supposed to” (Du sollst kommen), “sollen” has a subjective meaning: you report what OTHERS say, without guaranteeing that it's true.
The restaurant is said to be very good.
It's supposed to rain tomorrow. (according to the forecast)
It's the equivalent of “Man sagt, dass er reich ist” or “Angeblich ist er reich”, but shorter and very common in the press.
Subjective “wollen”: the person states something ABOUT THEMSELVES, and you have your doubts.
He claims not to have known anything.
3. The past: soll / will + participle + haben / sein
For something that happened in the past, the modal stays in the present, and the past infinitive (participle + haben / sein) comes at the end:
Er soll zehn Häuser gekauft haben.
Das Haus soll verkauft worden sein.
“Er sollte kommen” = he was supposed to come (objective). “Er soll gekommen sein” = he is said to have come (subjective). The difference is in the infinitive at the end.
In the news you'll often hear the combination: “Der Täter soll… Laut Polizei soll er…” = The offender reportedly… According to the police, he is said to have…

By the next morning the whole of Kastanienallee knew. Rumours travel faster than the tram in Prenzlauer Berg. The investor from Munich is said to own twenty houses, people were saying at the baker's. He's said to drive a Porsche, people said at the florist's. He's apparently already bought a whole street in Kreuzberg and thrown all the tenants out onto the street, Mrs Becker told everyone who bought a newspaper from her, and even those who didn't.

At number thirty-three there was panic. Mr Yilmaz hadn't slept all night. He worked as a bus driver, his wife as a cashier in a supermarket, and their three children went to the school on the corner. “Where are we supposed to go?” he asked Lena when he picked up his coffee in the morning. “A flat in Berlin for five people? It's impossible. We'd have to move to the edge of the city, and the children would have to change schools.”

And old Mrs Schulze, who had lived in the same ground-floor flat since 1968, sat at her table by the café window and stirred her cup without drinking. “I'm eighty-eight,” she said quietly to Lena. “If I have to leave here, I'll die. I know it.” Lena sat down next to her, held her hand and didn't know what to say.

Ludwig listened to everything and said little. He sat on his bench, with Fritz at his feet, and thought. Klaus sat down next to him. “What are you thinking about?” he asked. “I'm thinking about a boy,” said Ludwig. “A boy who lived in our building thirty years ago. He's said to have moved to southern Germany later, someone told me. But that was a long time ago. And Michael is a common name. It's probably someone else.” It didn't sound as if he believed it himself.

At eleven o'clock a car stopped in front of number thirty-three. It wasn't a Porsche. It was an old green estate car with a child seat on the back seat. A man got out, about forty-five, with glasses and a plain grey jumper. He didn't look like an investor. He looked like a teacher. He stood on the pavement for a long time and looked up, not at number thirty-three, but at the building next door. At number thirty-one.

Ludwig was sitting, as he did every morning, on the bench in front of the café, with Fritz at his feet. The man walked slowly towards him. He stopped in front of him and at first said nothing. Then he said, his voice trembling a little: “Mr Brandt? You probably don't remember me. I'm Michael. Michael Kühn. I lived on the third floor from 1996 to 2001. With my mother.”

Ludwig looked at him for a long time. Then he slowly took off his glasses, wiped them with his handkerchief and put them back on. He saw a man of forty-five. But behind the glasses and the greying hair he suddenly saw a ten-year-old boy who sat on the stairs every afternoon, because his mother had to work till eight in the evening and he didn't have a key.
Little Michael. The boy on the stairs. Ingrid took you in every day. You did your homework at our place and drank cocoa.

And she taught me to read. Properly. At school they said I was stupid. At ten I could barely read. Mrs Brandt read with me for an hour every day. A whole year. She never said I was stupid. She said I just hadn't come across the right book yet.

Ludwig nodded slowly. “I remember. The first book you read on your own was «Emil und die Detektive» (Emil and the Detectives). You read it aloud to her on the last day before the summer holidays, all of it, from the first page to the last. It took four hours. Ingrid cried afterwards. She said it was the best day of her whole career. And then you moved away, you and your mother, and we never heard anything from you again.”

Meanwhile Lena and Klaus had come out of the café, and behind them stood Mr Yilmaz, suspicious, with his arms crossed. Mrs Schulze had come to the door too, leaning on her walking frame. Michael looked at them all and understood at once. “You've heard the rumours,” he said. “I'm supposed to want to throw out all the tenants, right? I'm supposed to collect houses the way other people collect stamps.”
Well, yes. Mrs Becker says you've apparently already bought twenty houses.

Mrs Becker! Is she still around? Back in 1998 she was telling everyone my mother was a Russian princess. No. I've bought exactly one house. This one. With the money left to me by my father, whom I never knew. I'm a teacher in Munich. A primary school teacher. For children who can't read well.

He paused and smiled awkwardly. “I always wanted to write to you, Mr Brandt. Every year at Christmas I started a card. And every year I thought: you've probably forgotten me. What do you write to a woman who gave you the most important thing in your life? Thank you is too little. And then, three years ago, I found out she had died. Too late. I came too late.”

It went very quiet on Kastanienallee. Even Fritz raised his head. Michael went on. Number thirty-three had belonged to a property company that really did want to renovate it and sell it at a high price. Michael had seen the advert by chance on the internet while looking for photos of his old street. He hadn't slept for three nights. Then he had rung the company and bought the house before anyone else could.

Nobody will be thrown out of here. Nobody. The rents stay as they are. I just want to repair the roof, because apparently it's been raining in for years, and the heating. And on the ground floor, where the coal cellar used to be, I'd like to set something up. A small room with books. For the children on the street who have nowhere to go after school.

Mr Yilmaz slowly uncrossed his arms. Mrs Schulze began to cry, quietly, without a sound. And Ludwig stood up, leaning on his walking stick, and hugged Michael, as he had never done thirty years before, because back then it wasn't done, a man and a boy from the stairs.
What do you want to call it? The book room?
I was thinking… if you don't mind… “Ingrid's Reading Corner”.

At first Ludwig couldn't answer. Then he just said: “She would have laughed. And then she would have said that you have to choose the first book.” Michael laughed. “I already know. «Emil und die Detektive». What else?” Lena looked at her grandfather and saw that he was laughing and crying at the same time, and thought that she had never seen him like that before.

In the afternoon Klaus went to the kiosk and, for the first time in years, bought a newspaper from Mrs Becker. “Have you heard?” she asked at once. “The investor is said to…” “Mrs Becker,” Klaus interrupted her kindly. “This time I'll tell you a story. And this one is true.” And Mrs Becker listened, for the first time in forty years, without interrupting even once. The next day the whole of Kastanienallee knew. This time the rumour was the truth.
